message.content:
**Atomic‑mass units (amu)**  
| Particle | Mass (amu) |
|----------|------------|
| **Proton** | \(m_p \approx 1.007\,276\,466\,88\;\text{amu}\) |
| **Neutron** | \(m_n \approx 1.008\,664\,916\,00\;\text{amu}\) |

These are the most recent CODATA‐recommended values (the difference between them is only about \(0.00139\;\text{amu}\), i.e., roughly one part per thousand).

---

### “Size” – Effective Diameter  

Because protons and neutrons are composite particles made of quarks bound by gluons, there isn’t a sharp surface like a classical sphere. In practice physicists quote *root‑mean‑square* radii derived from scattering experiments, then sometimes convert those into an equivalent “effective diameter.” Typical values used in nuclear physics texts are:

| Particle | RMS Radius (fm) | Approximate Effective Diameter (≈ 2×RMS) |
|----------|-----------------|-------------------------------------------|
| **Proton** | \(r_{\!p}^{\rm rms} \simeq 0.87~{\rm fm}\) | \(\sim 1.74~{\rm fm}\) |
| **Neutron** | \(r_{n}^{\rm rms} \simeq 0.85~{\rm fm}\) | \(\sim 1.70~{\rm fm}\) |

> **Why this number?**  
> - These radii come from elastic electron–proton scattering data (for the proton) and parity‑violating neutrino/neutron scattering or other indirect methods (for the neutron).  
> - The quoted “diameter’’ is simply twice the rms radius—an intuitive way to think about how far the strong force extends when two nucleons interact. It’s not a hard boundary, but it gives you a useful scale for nuclear forces (~1–2 fm).

So, summarizing:

- **Masses:** \(m_p \approx 1.00728\;\text{amu}\); \(m_n \approx 1.00866\;\text{amu}\).
- **Effective Diameters:** about \(1.7\;\text{fm}\) each (roughly \(10^{-15}\,\text{m}\)).
